paras: The lynching of Gibbon took place at Rock Creek, Albany County, Wyoming Territory, on the evening of August 21, 1882, when citizens hanged a hunter named Gibbon from a railroad box car hours after he was accused of shooting a store clerk, Robert Aiken. No one is reported to have been arrested for the hanging, and the Laramie dispatch on it ran widely under the heading "Lynch Law." None of the reports gives the race of Gibbon, Aiken or the men who hanged him.

Robert Aiken was one of three clerks in the Rock Creek store of Chas. E. Clay, whom the Cheyenne Daily Leader called "our former townsman." According to the Leader, Gibbon came into the store "much the worse for the liquor he had taken in" and fell into "a wordy quarrel," during which he drew a revolver and shot Aiken, who died almost at once. A North Carolina crime column said instead that Aiken had "refused him liquor," and a Dakota paper called Aiken a "barkeeper."

The Laramie dispatch put the shooting after 5 p.m. and said that between 9 and 10 o'clock that night "citizens took Gibbon out and hung him to a box car." In the Leader's account, bystanders gave Gibbon "a thorough mauling," after which "an assembled crowd" took him to a box car nearby, ran a plank out from its roof, and hanged him from it until he was dead. A facetious letter from Wyoming printed in October said the townspeople bound the man hand and foot and set a guard over him while a "committee" decided against a telegraph pole and chose a box car on the side track.

Aiken's body passed through Cheyenne on August 23 on its way to his parents' home at "Caliope," Iowa, and the Laramie Boomerang, as quoted by the Leader, called him a young man who "was never quarrelsome" and said his murder "was entirely unprovoked." The only mention of an inquest is in the October letter, which said the coroner found that the dead man had died from "falling from a box car, caused by the lack of rope." No report of an arrest or prosecution of any of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Cheyenne Daily Leader approved of the hanging, heading its report "LYNCHED. Speedy Justice Done a Cold Blooded Murderer at Rock Creek" and opening with "Western Wyoming is the place for speedy and effective justice." The Laramie wire dispatch ran on August 23 in the St. Paul Daily Globe, the New-York Tribune and other dailies, and a day later in the Helena Weekly Herald, under headings such as "Lynch Law" and "MURDER AND LYNCH LAW," without comment. Condensed versions then went into weekly news roundups as far away as Arkansas, North Carolina and Nebraska through the end of August, one remarking that "The murderer was informally hanged."

Some papers treated the hanging as a joke. The Carson City Morning Appeal described men "in disguise" hanging a man from "a baggage car" and said Laramie, offended at not being invited to the "masquerade," threatened to hang its own postmaster. In October the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo printed a letter signed "Ed. Walsh" that called the lynchers a "committee of humorists" and the hanging "a grand success." The Press and Daily Dakotaian credited the hanging to "The 3-7-77's," a name it also gave in the same column to a vigilance group at Billings, Montana.

Accounts differ on where Gibbon was held: one wire summary said citizens took him "out of jail" and another that he "was arrested," while the Wyoming accounts described townspeople seizing and guarding him at the scene. Some shorter reports also placed the event at Laramie or even "Laramie City. Neb.," but the full Laramie dispatch and the Cheyenne paper both put it at Rock Creek, with Laramie only the dateline.
